_help: The story, by day (chapter) and room: docs/STORY.md. Each day walks the seven rooms in route order and is one period of Céline's life (Day 1 newest, Day 3 oldest). Per room: title and years (the room card when it starts, and the scrapbook), intro (one line on the card), outro (on the way to the next room), memories (the notes: a level's note with "memory": id takes its text from here). Day intro/title/years are on the Day card at the start of each day.

chapters.title: The summers with Juliette
chapters.intro: Mamie's last years, and all the summers you spent here.

rooms.title: Mornings with Chloé
rooms.intro: Mamie's last years: the sunrise walk, the market, coffee at this table.
rooms.outro: The door to the hall swings open. Somewhere a floorboard creaks.

memories.title: Welcome home
memories.text:
Ma chérie Juliette,
Welcome home. Yes, home: the house is yours now. You know I can't give anything without a riddle, so I made you one last treasure hunt, through the house and back through my life. It takes three mornings. Good things take their time.
The first one is easy. My Saturday market list, the same every week: 3 lemons, 1 little cheese for Chloé, 7 peaches. The kitchen drawers open with my list, in that order.
Take your time. The sun isn't up yet.
Mamie

memories.title: Look after Chloé
memories.text:
Juliette, one more thing, the most important one. Chloé will be hiding somewhere in the house. She does that when she misses someone. She's shy the first time, but she can never resist Gaston, her squeaky seagull. Once she trusts you, she'll follow you everywhere and poke her nose into everything. Please look after her for me. Breakfast at 8.
Mamie

memories.title: The lemon tart
memories.text:
Lemon tart, the one you always ask for.
Three lemons from the market (never from the supermarket, they sulk), butter, sugar, eggs, and patience.
The secret is to take it out while the middle still trembles a little. Like me on the scales at the doctor's.
Make it for someone. It tastes better that way.

rooms.title: Every summer, a little taller
rooms.intro: Every summer you came back a little taller, and the hall knew it first.
rooms.outro: The little gate at the foot of the stairs swings open.

memories.title: The pencil marks
memories.text:
Every first day of summer you stood against the door frame, heels to the wall, and I drew a line with a little number next to it. Every summer you stood on your toes, and every summer I pretended not to see.
I'll always remember those first three measurements we took.
Mamie

memories.title: The first bus
memories.text:
You always came with the bus, every summer, your bucket on your knees and your nose on the window. But we forgot what time you came, because the clock stopped working the summer you stopped coming every year.
Maybe you can fix it again.

memories.title: Our summers
memories.text: Our summers stood in a row, oldest first, until a small white dog decided otherwise. The first summer you only cared about shells for your castle. The next, the sea finally let you in. The summer of the shooting stars came after that. And last of all, the summer you only cared about that boy at the ice-cream stand. Don't blush.

memories.title: The shoebox
memories.text: Found in the pocket of Mamie's old cardigan, under Chloé: "I kept every treasure hunt I ever made you, in the shoebox on top of the wardrobe. When this one is all over, have a look. Some of them are very hard. You were very clever, even at six."

rooms.title: Thunderstorm nights
rooms.intro: When the thunder came, you came padding in here with your pillow.
rooms.outro: Down the stairs, through the hall, into the living room.

memories.title: The lullaby
memories.text:
When the thunder came, you padded in with your pillow and your serious face, and I sang the only song I know by heart. First the little star comes out, then the little wave rocks the boat, and the little shell keeps the sea until morning.
You never once heard the end.

memories.title: The counting book
memories.text: Our counting book, for storm nights. You made me promise: one sheep for every star on your wall, and two kisses for every sheep. You were always asleep before the kisses. I gave them anyway.

memories.title: The storm drawing
memories.text: Under Chloé's paws, a child's drawing: a house, a very big moon, and two people in one bed. On the back, in Mamie's writing: "The night of the big storm. You said the thunder was only the sky moving its furniture."

rooms.title: Rainy days
rooms.intro: Rainy days: forts, number squares, and cards Mamie always lost.
rooms.outro: The garden doors open onto wet grass.

memories.title: The fort rules
memories.text:
The rules of the fort, by Juliette, aged eight, in felt pen:
It has to be night inside, so no sunshine.
But not without the stars.
The shells only glow when the stars do.
The sea is never where the shells are.
(Mamie is allowed in if she brings biscuits.)

memories.title: The grey squares
memories.text: Every rainy day ended the same way: you finished the number square, and whatever was in the grey squares, read like a book, was your pocket money. It went straight into the middle of the long sideboard, where I kept the biscuit money. You never once let me finish one.

memories.title: Mamie at cards
memories.text: For the record: I did not lose at cards every rainy day. I lost at cards every day. You kept score on the fridge, in felt pen, and you never once let me forget it.

rooms.title: The red bicycle
rooms.intro: Up and down the garden path on a red bicycle.
rooms.outro: The blue shed door creaks open.

memories.title: The red bicycle
memories.text: The summer of the red bicycle: up and down this path all day. You fell off once for every daisy in my jam jar, and got back on every single time, while every little bird on the trellis had something to say about it. The garden table remembers every fall.

memories.title: The crab
memories.text:
The crab in the rock pool pinched you just as the church bells finished ringing nine, and you cried until they rang the half hour. Henri's shadow clock in the garden still remembers that morning.
It only needs reminding.

memories.title: The garden hose
memories.text: The summer you were in charge of watering: you watered the tomatoes, then me, then the cat next door and, for some reason, the letterbox. We laughed until we had to sit down in the wet grass.

rooms.title: Bucket and spade
rooms.intro: Your first summers: a bucket, a spade, and a great many shells.
rooms.outro: The side gate leads round to the front garden.

memories.title: The shell counts
memories.text:
Your first summers, the little red bucket came everywhere, full of shells. Every evening we counted them out on this workbench and I wrote the number on its lid, so you could beat it tomorrow.
You never did beat that very first day.

memories.title: The ribbons
memories.text: You never won the sandcastle contest, but you got a ribbon every year for the most shells. I made sure of that. The red bicycle came the summer after your very first ribbon, and you rode it straight into the roses.

memories.title: The contest rules
memories.text: The sandcastle contest rules, in your handwriting, stuck to the shed wall: 1. A moat. 2. Shells on everything. 3. Mamie is not allowed to help. (Mamie helped.)

rooms.title: You came
rooms.intro: The summer after Henri. The day you first came through this gate.
rooms.outro: The sun is up. The first day is done.

memories.title: The drawings
memories.text: That first summer you drew a picture for Papa Henri every single day and posted it yourself. You wrote our house number twice on every envelope, because once wasn't polite enough for heaven.

memories.title: You came
memories.text:
The summer after Henri, you arrived at this gate with a bucket, a very serious face and a list: hopscotch, swing, ice cream, Mamie. We did all of it that same afternoon.
Everything you gave me that summer is in this bucket. You saved me, ma puce.

memories.title: The ice-cream
memories.text: One ice cream a day, that was the rule. By the second week you had talked it up to two, and by August the man at the kiosk handed you a cone before you'd even asked. You had that effect on people.

memories.title: The first walk
memories.text: Your first evening here you insisted on walking me to the market "so I wouldn't get lost". It's round the corner. You held my hand the whole way and told everyone we met that I was your Mamie.

chapters.title: Henri and Margot
chapters.intro: Henri, Margot, and the first years in this house.

rooms.title: Breakfast for two
rooms.intro: Henri's number puzzle, Mamie's crossword, and too much coffee.
rooms.outro: The hall is quiet this morning.

memories.title: The crossword
memories.text: Every breakfast for forty years: Henri at that end with his number puzzle, me at this end with the crossword, and we cheated for each other. His favourite clue was always the same one: the year we met, one Saturday at the stall. I always pretended I'd forgotten it. He always looked at the old calendar anyway.

memories.title: Henri's coffee
memories.text: Henri was a harbour master even at breakfast. The coffee went on at six o'clock sharp, and he wouldn't pour a drop until every boat in the harbour photo had gone out: one minute for each. The kitchen clock never dared to disagree.

memories.title: Henri's cup
memories.text: Henri's cup still hangs on its hook. I use it on Sundays, and I cheat at the crossword for him.

memories.title: Sunday pancakes
memories.text: On Sunday mornings Henri made pancakes in the shape of the countries we'd seen. They all came out looking like Portugal. We ate Portugal every Sunday for twenty years.

rooms.title: The quiet house
rooms.intro: Margot left for Montréal, and the telephone in the hall rang every Sunday.
rooms.outro: Up the stairs, to their room.

memories.title: Margot leaves
memories.text: The morning Margot left for Montréal she was eighteen, with the big suitcase and her father's patience. She left her little hospital bracelet in the shell bowl, for luck, and of course she forgot it.

memories.title: Sunday calls
memories.text: After she left, the telephone in the hall rang every Sunday: breakfast time in Montréal, lunch time here. Margot never once got the hours right, so her father wrote them down for her and put the card in the old clock, where the ticking would keep it safe.

memories.title: The travel suitcase
memories.text: In those quiet years the suitcase by the door was never quite unpacked. When the house was too quiet, we went and watched the sun come up somewhere else. Santorini was the best one.

rooms.title: Dancing in socks
rooms.intro: The house was quiet again. Number puzzles, dancing in socks, and trips at last.
rooms.outro: Down the stairs, through the hall, into the living room.

memories.title: Our song
memories.text: On Sunday mornings Henri wound up the little box on my dressing table and asked me to dance, in our socks, on the creaky floor. Our song always began with love, of course. The sunshine came just before the stars, and the sea never had the last word.

memories.title: The suitcase
memories.text: Every sticker on this suitcase is a sunrise we watched together. His good jacket, the one from our wedding, still hangs with the Sunday clothes. It was only ever allowed out once a year: on the anniversary of the day in the photo above the bed.

memories.title: Henri's last puzzle
memories.text: Every morning Henri did the number puzzle and I did the crossword, and we cheated for each other. This was his last one, half done. I never had the heart to finish it. He always shaded the squares he liked best, read them like a book, and kept whatever they said by the bed with his glasses.

rooms.title: Margot
rooms.intro: The family years: Sunday records, birthday cakes and stories under the lamp.
rooms.outro: The garden doors open onto the morning.

memories.title: Story time
memories.text:
The rules for story time, by Margot, aged seven:
The sun lamp is on, because it's the reading lamp.
The stars sleep while Papa reads.
The shells are on whenever the sun is.
The sea is only on when the stars are off.
(Papa must do the voices properly.)

memories.title: Sunday records
memories.text: Margot's secret hiding place, behind the books! In her round handwriting: "Papa's Sunday records, the way he always plays them: the dancing one last, under the stars. The sunny one straight after the sea song. And never the sad love song first, Maman says it's too sad for the morning."

memories.title: Birthdays
memories.text: Margot's birthdays in this room: a cake with too many candles, a fort made of every cushion in the house, and one year a very surprised tortoise. She hated her piano lessons. Then one day she didn't. I never found out why, and I never asked.

rooms.title: The first years
rooms.intro: A wedding under a lemon tree so small it needed a stick to stand up.
rooms.outro: The blue shed door creaks open.

memories.title: Under the lemon tree
memories.text: We married right here on 18 June 1960, under a lemon tree so small it needed a stick to stand up. Henri checked his watch just as I said yes, of course: the big hand on the nine, the little one nearly at eleven. The garden has kept our time ever since.

memories.title: The first spring
memories.text: Our first spring, the seed jars in the order we sowed them: the green beans first, Henri insisted. The tomatoes, red as hearts, went in just before the sunflowers. The radishes, pale as shells, were never last: they're far too impatient.

memories.title: The first lemon
memories.text: The first lemon from our tree, summer 1961. It was tiny and very sour and we ate it anyway, at the little table, one half each. Our only guests were the daisies in the jar and the birds on the trellis, and we only had the two chairs.

memories.title: The stick
memories.text: The stick that held up the lemon tree is still tied to its trunk. Henri said it could come off when the tree was taller than me. It still hasn't come off. I think we both liked it there.

rooms.title: Henri's blue shed
rooms.intro: Henri painted the shed blue and built everything in it.
rooms.outro: The side gate leads round to the front garden.

memories.title: Sea blue
memories.text: Henri painted this shed blue the summer after we married, the colour of the sea at seven in the morning. He wrote on the pot when he finished, so he could buy the same blue again, and put his brushes away in his right-hand drawer. He never needed more. This blue has lasted.

memories.title: The cradle
memories.text: Henri built Margot's cradle on this bench from the wood of his old rowing boat. He carved a little wave on it for every month we waited for her, and a star for each of the three of us. It went to Montréal with her, but I can still count them with my eyes shut. So could the little cart by the door.

memories.title: The bench
memories.text: Henri built the garden bench in here too, and carried it out on his back the day Margot learned to walk, so she'd have somewhere to walk to.

rooms.title: The key
rooms.intro: The day Maman gave them the house, and the day they carried Margot home.
rooms.outro: The sun is up. The second day is done.

memories.title: Margot comes home
memories.text: We carried Margot home through this gate on the first warm morning of spring, and Henri hung a swing on the old pine the very next day. He carved her name and the year into the seat, so it would never forget her. Maman's little post box by the gate has kept that year ever since.

memories.title: Maman's letter
memories.text: Maman's letter, the day we came home from Lisbon: "The house is yours now. The key is where you always hid your treasures, under my roses, in the little box with our number on it. Don't let Henri dig: he'll pull them all up."

memories.title: Over the step
memories.text: Henri carried me over the step when we came home from Lisbon, and dropped me straight into Maman's roses. He said it was tradition. It was not.

chapters.title: The girl at the flower stall
chapters.intro: The girl at the flower stall, and the little girl by the sea.

rooms.title: One vase
rooms.intro: One vase on Maman's kitchen table, and a sunflower in it every Saturday.
rooms.outro: The hall, and the letterbox slot in the front door.

memories.title: One vase
memories.text: One vase on Maman's kitchen table, and every Saturday for a whole year a sunflower in it, from a young sailor who swore they were for his mother. When he finally sailed, on a ship called the Aurore, he gave me his cabin number, as if I might come looking. Nine. His photo lived in two halves until he came back.

memories.title: The market money
memories.text: Maman never wrote anything down twice. What mattered went into the grey squares of her number puzzle, read like a book, and then into the spoons' drawer with the market money. Nothing was ever lost.

memories.title: Saturdays
memories.text: Saturdays at the stall began in this kitchen at five: bread, coffee, and Maman's voice counting buckets. I thought everyone's mother counted buckets. Then I met Henri's.

rooms.title: Letters through the door
rooms.intro: Henri's letters from the sea, through the slot in the front door.
rooms.outro: Up the stairs, to her old room.

memories.title: Letters from the sea
memories.text: Henri's letters came through the slot in the front door, tied with string. Every one began the same way: "On the Aurore it is morning, at the hour of my cabin, and I am thinking of you." And every one ended: "Keep one sunflower for me."

memories.title: Days at sea (torn)
memories.text: Half a letter, torn along the fold: "...counted every day on the way to Japan: seventy of them..."

memories.title: Days at sea (the other half)
memories.text: The other half, from the basket by the door: "...and seventy-seven on the way back, because I missed you, and because the captain got lost."

rooms.title: The window
rooms.intro: Céline's girlhood room, and the window where she watched for Papa's boat.
rooms.outro: Down the stairs, through the hall.

memories.title: Maman's song
memories.text: Maman sang me to sleep in this room with the very song I later sang to you. Only she sang it the other way round: from the morning back to the night. She said it made the sunrise come quicker.

memories.title: Papa's boat (torn)
memories.text: Half a page from my diary: "Papa left for the sea every morning at twenty..."

memories.title: Papa's boat (the other half)
memories.text: The other half, from under the bed: "...to six. From this window I waved until I couldn't see his lamp any more."

rooms.title: Evenings by the radio
rooms.intro: Evenings by the radio with Maman.
rooms.outro: Out into Maman's garden.

memories.title: The radio
memories.text: The winter Papa didn't come back from the sea, Maman and I sat by the radio every evening anyway. We weren't waiting any more; we just liked the voices. She wrote the stations on the little blackboard, one after another, always three apart, and then stopped: I finished them for her.

memories.title: Three books
memories.text: Every winter Maman read me the same three stories, always in the same order: the one about the stars first, because it got dark so early; the sea one when the storms came; and the garden one last, to bring the spring back.

memories.title: The voices
memories.text: The man who read the sea forecast had the kindest voice in the world. Maman said he sounded like a lighthouse. I never found out his name. I didn't want to.

rooms.title: Maman's flower beds
rooms.intro: The flower beds that filled the stall at the market.
rooms.outro: The old shed door creaks open.

memories.title: Maman's rows
memories.text: Maman planted her flower beds like a song: sunflowers, roses, green leaves for the bouquets, and again, and again, row after row. Whatever the rows said, the stall sold out by noon.

memories.title: Cutting time (torn)
memories.text: Half of Maman's garden list: "Saturdays: cut the flowers at half past..."

memories.title: Cutting time (the other half)
memories.text: The other half, folded small under the stone of the bird bath: "...five, with the dew still on them, or they sulk."

memories.title: Bouquets
memories.text: Maman could tie a bouquet with one hand and give change with the other. I never learned the first. I was very good at the second.

memories.title: Maman's hat
memories.text: Maman's straw hat hung on the shed door all summer. When it was gone from the hook, she was at the stall. When it was back, she was home. I told the time by that hat.

rooms.title: The girl at the flower stall
rooms.intro: One sunflower, every Saturday, for a whole year.
rooms.outro: The side door leads round to the front of the house, where it all began.

memories.title: One sunflower
memories.text: Maman's price board from the flower stall. A young sailor bought one sunflower every Saturday for a whole year. I thought he had a lot of vases. He had one. When I got my delivery bicycle that summer, I gave its little lock his sunflowers, and then the day in June I would marry him, though I didn't know it yet.

memories.title: Maman's scales
memories.text: Maman weighed everything twice. She had three weights, and she made me learn them by heart before I could touch the till: all three together, eleven kilos. The middle one, a kilo more than the small one. The big one, as heavy as two middle ones. Smallest first, every morning, at the bench where she counted the money.

memories.title: The flower cart
memories.text: Maman's cart went down to the market every Saturday before dawn, and I pushed it back up every afternoon. It squeaked on the left. It still does. I never oiled it: that squeak was the sound of Saturday.

memories.title: My first Saturday
memories.text: My first Saturday alone at the stall I was seventeen, I sold everything by ten, and I gave the last bunch of sweet peas to a man who said it was for his mother. It wasn't Henri. Henri came later, and he was worse at lying.

rooms.title: Where it began
rooms.intro: A little girl ran down this path every morning to wave at her father's boat.
rooms.outro: The gate opens. The sun is up.

memories.title: Waving at Papa
memories.text: Every morning Papa left for the sea before dawn, and every morning I ran down this path in my nightdress to wave at his boat as the sun came up. That's where it started, ma puce: me and the sunrise. Maman kept her old dog's leash behind a number only we knew: our house, and then the last square I ever reached at hopscotch.

memories.title: Maman's roses
memories.text: Maman planted these roses by the gate the year I was born. She said a house should smell nice when you come home, even if you only went to the market.

memories.title: The time capsule
memories.text: A biscuit tin, rusty at the edges. I buried it under Maman's roses when I was ten years old, with a shell, a marble and a drawing of the sun. The gate has kept that year for me. The last letter is inside the tin, under the shell and the marble.

memories.title: The marble
memories.text: The marble in the tin was the best one in the whole street. I won it from Émile Martin, who cried, and I nearly gave it back. Nearly.
